children.text: Miyamoto keeps singing "will we be here [forever]", over and over again, but this iteration comes across as an angry outburst. So many times of holding back, "Gaman", but finally, she cannot hold her patience anymore; everything that Japanese Americans had tried to do to ensure their loyalty to the United States had failed. Around this time stamp, Miyamoto lists out the location of every internment camp while continuing to sing "will we be here [forever]".

This part that the piano plays is repeated throughout the song, usually when Miyamoto sings "Will we be here all our lives?". This repeated piano segment portrays the uncertainty, fear and confusion that Miyamoto felt when she was in the U.S internment camp. She shapes memory through this repetition, especially when it gets stronger each time.

The continuous cutback to the grave while Nobuko is listing the different names of the Japanese American internment camps across the US. This reveals how the pain and suffering was felt throughout all camps and takes the form of a physical tomb etched into the ground. Although the lives of those in the camps were lost, they were perhaps able to escape the immense suffering they experienced “To Die Is Gain”.

A low whisper saying “never again” conveys a very somber message that the memories of the lives the Japanese people in those camps had before they entered the camps can never be relived. I also interpreted this whisper as a strong message to listeners never to forget what happened in these camps: keep the message of this song alive in our own memory to ensure nothing like this happens again.

Miyamoto lists the names of the internment camps in a vocal tone that suggests restraint. In highlighting the scope of the many camps, she carries the collective memory of Japanese Americans in her music, and "Gaman" becomes a testimony for shared cultural memory rather than a song about solely her own story. At the same time, her restrained tone suggests that she is trying to impart dignity into her description of Japanese American history, asserting agency when talking about events that attempted to dehumanize her community.

Miyamoto uses the repetitive lyrics of "120,000 stories" to really emphasize how truly devastating it is that this has happened to the Japanese Americans in the WWII war and that each and individual soldier had a story, a life, a family, a meaning. This repetition is also emphasizing that this war and the concentration camps was a true show of the abuse of power by the elite to utilize innocent lives for trivial matters. It also shows how dark humanity can be to each other regardless of reason.

Miyamoto begins the outro of the song with the title "Gaman." In the midst of the tragedy and suffering, the Japanese Americans tell themselves to endure the oppression. This is the only way they can preserve their identity, and carry on/continue to build their legacy. The title being in Japanese specifically captured the essence of holding onto culture intentionally.

The term "Gaman" is to endure te impossible with patience and endurance. From the artist repeating "will we be here all our lives?" to the an of the little girl trapped in the room and then finally the message of gaman. This can be interpreted from the oung childs point of view asking naiive questions and simply wantg to be free. The message of gaman is for the children especially and for all of the people to stay strong throughout this hardship.

Miyamoto repeats what she says in the beginning: "A hundred twenty thousand stories...". I feel like the reiteration of these couple of sentences is structured perfectly, as it lets the audience know again why these stories must never be forgotten. There is a stress specifically in the number "120,000" because Miyamoto wants people to know that a large number of lives were affected, not only hers. The only difference in this reiteration is that in the last 3 seconds of the video, Miyamoto says the words "never again". Miyamoto thinks about memories that have been buried, but also thinks about a new beginning where this injustice should never take place again.

I notice that Miyamoto's voice becomes more emotional and intense in this moment. The repetition and pacing make the memory feel heavy and difficult to leave behind. The voice not only tells us about the past; it makes the past feel present.
